content: The innate immune system consists of cells and mechanisms that provide the host with defense against infections caused by other organisms in a non-specific manner. This means that the cells of the innate immune system recognize and respond to pathogens in a general way, but unlike the adaptive immune system, it does not provide long-lasting or protective immunity to the host. The innate immune system offers immediate defense against infections and is present in all classes of plant and animal life. The innate immune system is considered an evolutionarily older defense strategy and is the predominant immune system in plants, fungi, insects, and primitive multicellular organisms. In vertebrates, the major functions of the innate immune system include recruiting immune cells to sites of infection and inflammation through the production of chemical factors such as cytokines, activating the complement cascade to identify bacteria and promote the clearance of dead cells or antibody complexes, identifying and removing foreign substances in organs, tissues, blood, and lymph via specialized white blood cells, and activating the adaptive immune system through antigen presentation. Inflammation is one of the first responses of the immune system to infection or irritation. It is triggered by chemical factors released by injured cells and serves to establish a physical barrier against the spread of infection while promoting the healing of damaged tissue after pathogen clearance. Chemical factors such as histamine, bradykinin, serotonin, and leukotrienes produced during inflammation sensitize pain receptors, cause vasodilation of blood vessels at the site, and attract phagocytes, especially neutrophils. Neutrophils then release factors that summon other leukocytes and lymphocytes, amplifying the immune response. The inflammatory response is characterized by redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor), and potential dysfunction of the affected organs or tissues (functio laesa). The complement system is a biochemical cascade within the immune system that enhances the ability of antibodies to clear pathogens or mark them for destruction by other cells. This cascade is composed of plasma proteins synthesized in the liver, primarily by hepatocytes. These proteins work together to recruit inflammatory cells, tag pathogens for destruction through opsonization, disrupt the plasma membrane of infected cells (causing cytolysis), and remove neutralized antigen-antibody complexes. Elements of the complement cascade are found in many species, including plants, birds, fish, and some invertebrates. All white blood cells (WBCs), also known as leukocytes, are part of the innate immune response. Unlike other cells in the body, leukocytes are not tightly associated with specific organs or tissues and function similarly to independent, single-celled organisms. They can move freely, interact with, and capture cellular debris, foreign particles, or invading microorganisms. Most innate immune leukocytes cannot divide or reproduce independently but are produced by pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow. Innate leukocytes include natural killer cells, mast cells, eosinophils, basophils, and phagocytic cells such as macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells. These cells identify and eliminate pathogens that may cause infection. Mast cells are a type of innate immune cell found in connective tissue and mucous membranes. They play a role in defense against pathogens, wound healing, and are often associated with allergy and anaphylaxis. When activated, mast cells release granules rich in histamine and heparin, along with hormonal mediators and chemokines. Histamine dilates blood vessels, causing inflammation and recruiting neutrophils and macrophages to the site. Phagocytes, or eating cells, engulf and digest pathogens or particles. Once inside the cell, the pathogen is contained within an endosome, which merges with a lysosome containing enzymes and acids that kill and digest the pathogen. Phagocytes patrol the body for pathogens and respond to molecular signals called cytokines. Phagocytic cells include macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells. Phagocytosis also removes dead host cells, aiding in tissue maintenance and healing after injury. Macrophages, meaning large eating cells, are large phagocytic leukocytes capable of moving outside the vascular system to pursue invading pathogens. In tissues, macrophages differentiate from blood monocytes. They are highly efficient phagocytes, capable of engulfing large numbers of bacteria or other cells. Bacterial molecules binding to macrophage surface receptors trigger the engulfment and destruction of bacteria through a respiratory burst, releasing reactive oxygen species. Macrophages also produce chemokines to recruit other immune cells to the infection site. Neutrophils, a type of granulocyte, contain granules in their cytoplasm and have lobed nuclei. Their granules contain toxic substances that kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria and fungi. Like macrophages, neutrophils attack pathogens by activating a respiratory burst, producing strong oxidizing agents such as hydrogen peroxide, free oxygen radicals, and hypochlorite. Neutrophils are the most abundant type of phagocyte, representing 50-60% of circulating leukocytes, and are usually the first cells to arrive at an infection site. The bone marrow of a healthy adult produces over 100 billion neutrophils daily, with production increasing during acute inflammation. Dendritic cells (DCs) are phagocytic cells found in tissues in contact with the external environment, such as the skin (where they are called Langerhans cells) and mucosal linings of the nose, lungs, stomach, and intestines. They are named for their resemblance to neuronal dendrites but are not connected to the nervous system. Dendritic cells are crucial for antigen presentation, linking the innate and adaptive immune systems. Basophils and eosinophils are related to neutrophils. Basophils release histamine when activated by pathogens, playing a role in defense against parasites and allergic reactions such as asthma. Eosinophils secrete toxic proteins and free radicals effective against bacteria and parasites but can also cause tissue damage during allergic reactions. Their activation and toxin release are tightly regulated to prevent inappropriate tissue destruction. Natural killer (NK) cells are part of the innate immune system and attack host cells infected by microbes or tumor cells. They do not directly attack microbes but destroy infected or abnormal host cells through a process called missing-self, targeting cells with low levels of the MHC I marker. NK cells were named for their ability to kill cells without prior activation. γδ T cells exhibit characteristics of both innate and adaptive immunity. They rearrange TCR genes to produce diversity and develop memory phenotypes, aligning with adaptive immunity. However, they also use restricted TCRs or NK receptors as pattern recognition receptors, responding rapidly to microbial molecules or stressed epithelial cells. Pathogens have evolved mechanisms to evade the innate immune system, such as intracellular replication (e.g., Salmonella), protective capsules (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis), or inhibition of phagocytosis. Some bacteria mimic host cells to avoid recognition, while others, like Staphylococcus aureus, inhibit phagocyte responses. Biofilms formed by bacteria and fungi provide protection from immune cells and proteins, contributing to chronic infections. In prokaryotes, the restriction-modification system defends against bacteriophages by producing restriction endonucleases that destroy viral DNA. Host DNA is protected by methylation, marking it as self. Invertebrates lack lymphocytes and antibody-based immunity but possess mechanisms resembling precursors to vertebrate immunity. They use pattern recognition receptors, such as Toll-like receptors, to identify pathogens. The complement system and antimicrobial peptides, like defensins and cecropins, are key components of invertebrate immunity. Plants also face infections from bacteria, fungi, viruses, nematodes, and insects. They use complex metabolic responses to produce defensive chemicals and systemic signals to combat infections. Plants lack mobile immune cells but rely on pattern-recognition receptors and localized hypersensitive responses (HR) to prevent pathogen spread. HR involves rapid programmed cell death at the infection site. Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) renders the entire plant resistant to a broad spectrum of pathogens, involving chemical messengers like salicylic acid and jasmonic acid. RNA silencing mechanisms also block viral replication.
